belay.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: managing a rope (*belay your partner*), making a line fast (*belay the halyard*), and the Navy imperative *Belay that!*, which exists only as a command.
belay.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a climber or a line as object (*she belayed me on every pitch*), intransitive when the partner is understood (*he has belayed for beginners for six years*).
belay.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *I was belayed by my partner on every pitch*; *the halyard is belayed to a pin on the rail*. The imperative *Belay that!* has no passive.

clip.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: cutting (*clip the dog*), snipping out of print (*clip a coupon*), fastening (*clip the badge on*), striking in passing (*clip the curb*), and figurative curtailing (*clip his wings*).
clip.transitivity: **transitive** in all five senses, and the object is normally obligatory — ✗ *The truck clipped* is incomplete. The fastening sense adds a goal phrase: *clip A to B*.
clip.passive: **yes** — *his hair has been clipped the same way since 1998*; *a mic was clipped to his collar*; *his wings have been clipped since the merger*.

gainsay.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of speech, but so formal and frozen that it barely appears outside negative frames: *no one can gainsay it*, *there is no gainsaying it*.
gainsay.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory — a statement (*gainsay the numbers*) or a person (*gainsay the bishop*). ✗ *Nobody gainsaid* is incomplete.
gainsay.passive: **restricted** — natural only in the negative frames the verb lives in: *the finding has not been gainsaid in twenty years*. A plain positive passive sounds wrong: ✗ *Every point was gainsaid by the committee.*

have.verb type: **stative** in the core senses — possession (*we have two cars*), experience (*I had a headache*), obligation (*have to*) — and there it rejects the progressive: ✗ *I am having two cars*. **Dynamic** in the eat/drink, hold-an-event, give-birth and causative senses, where the progressive is fine: *we're having lunch*, *she's having a baby*. Also the **auxiliary** behind every perfect tense (*they have finished*).
have.transitivity: **transitive** in every full-verb sense, object obligatory — ✗ *We have* is incomplete. The causative takes object + complement: *have the roof replaced*, *have the office send you the file*. Never ditransitive. As auxiliary it takes no object at all, only a participle.
have.passive: **no** for the stative senses — this is the classic learner trap: ✗ *Two cars are had by us*, ✗ *A headache was had by me*, ✗ *A meeting is had every Monday*. The auxiliary has no passive either. The one live passive is the fixed idiom *be had* 'be cheated': *if you paid full price, you have been had*.

inlay.verb type: action — dynamic: setting one material flush into the surface of another (*inlay mother-of-pearl by hand*), including the dental sense (*inlay gold*).
inlay.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory, in two frames — *inlay A with B* (*inlay the wood with brass*) or *inlay B into A* (*inlay brass into the floor*).
inlay.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the commoner form — *every door in the house had been inlaid with ivory*; *brass letters have been inlaid into the lobby floor*. The participle doubles as an adjective: *an inlaid box*.

lay.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from putting something down flat to installing (*lay tile*), preparing (*lay a trap*), imposing (*lay blame*), and wagering (*lay fifty dollars*).
lay.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is what separates it from intransitive *lie*: ✗ *I laid down for a nap* should be *I lay down for a nap*. The one object-dropping sense is egg-laying: *the hens aren't laying*.
lay.passive: **yes** — *the tile had been laid before the inspector arrived*; *three charges were laid against the company*; *two hundred workers were laid off in March*.

make.verb type: action — dynamic in the creating, forcing, earning, and light-verb senses (*make a mistake*, *make a living*). The *amount to* sense is **stative** and copula-like, joining subject to a complement rather than acting on an object: *four quarters make a dollar*, *that makes nine of us* — no progressive, ✗ *four quarters are making a dollar*.
make.transitivity: **both**, and mostly transitive — plain transitive (*make coffee*), **ditransitive** (*make her a sandwich*), and complex-transitive with a complement (*make her chairman*, *make me happy*) or a bare infinitive (*they made him apologize*). Intransitive only inside the fixed *make do* and *make for*.
make.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the same part has been made there since 1962*; *she was made chief financial officer*. Note the shift in the forcing sense: the passive requires *to* — *he was made to apologize*, ✗ *he was made apologize*. **No** passive of the *amount to* sense: ✗ *A dollar is made by four quarters.*

mislay.verb type: action — dynamic, and narrower than *lose*: to put something down and forget where, with the expectation that it turns up.
mislay.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory — *mislay your glasses*, *mislay the tickets*. ✗ *He mislaid again* is incomplete.
mislay.passive: **yes** — *my file had been mislaid by the office, so I filled the form out twice*; *the spare key has been mislaid again*.

overflow.verb type: action — dynamic, and mostly a process rather than a deed: liquid spilling over (*the tub overflowed*), a space too full (*the meeting overflowed into the hallway*), feeling brimming over (*overflowing with gratitude*), and a buffer exceeding its space.
overflow.transitivity: **both** — normally intransitive, often with *into* (*the shelter has overflowed every night*), but transitive with the thing exceeded as object: *the creek overflowed its banks*, *the input overflowed the buffer*.
overflow.passive: **restricted** — no passive at all of the intransitive *the tub overflowed*. The transitive passive is standard only in computing and security writing: *the stack had been overflowed to run code*. With banks and levees it is marginal: ? *the levee was overflowed at three points*.

overlay.verb type: action — dynamic: putting one layer, image, or data set on top of another (*overlay the map with traffic data*), coating a surface (*overlay the wood with veneer*), and the figurative *politics overlays every decision here*.
overlay.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory, in the frame *overlay A with B* or *overlay B on A*. Careful: the intransitive-looking *the shale overlay the coal* is the past of a different verb, *overlie*.
overlay.passive: **yes**, and very common in the coating sense — *the dome is overlaid with gold leaf*; *the new route has been overlaid on the old survey*.

overpay.verb type: action — dynamic: paying more than a thing is worth (*overpay for cabs*), more than a person's work is worth (*overpay its back line*), or more than is actually owed.
overpay.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the seller, worker, or amount as object (*the city overpaid the contractor*), intransitive when the object is understood (*tourists always overpay*, *if you overpay, the balance rolls over*).
overpay.passive: **yes** with a person or a sum as object — *two executives were overpaid for years*; *the contractor was overpaid by nearly a million dollars*. The participle is a standard adjective: *an overpaid executive*. No passive of the intransitive *we overpaid for the house*.

pay.verb type: action — dynamic: handing over money (*pay the rent*), settling a debt, giving what is owed in attention or respect (*pay attention*, *pay a visit*), suffering consequences (*you'll pay for that*), and yielding a return (*the bond pays four percent*).
pay.transitivity: **ditransitive** at its core — *they paid her more than she asked for*, *pay him forty dollars* — and plain transitive with either object alone (*pay the fine*, *pay the servers*). **Intransitive** in the 'be profitable' sense: *it pays to read the fine print*, *the store never really paid*.
pay.passive: **yes**, with the recipient as the natural passive subject — *the servers are paid weekly*, *she was paid more than she asked for*; the sum promotes too: *the fine was paid without appeal*. **No** passive of the profitable sense: ✗ *It is paid to read the fine print.*

prepay.verb type: action — dynamic: paying before you receive or use something (*prepay the room*), or paying off a loan ahead of schedule (*prepay the mortgage*).
prepay.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the thing paid for as object (*we prepaid the shipping*), and the object drops freely when it is obvious (*guests can prepay online*).
prepay.passive: **yes** — *next year's insurance has been prepaid in full*; *the postage is prepaid on every return label*. The participle is far commoner as an adjective, with stress on the first syllable: *a prepaid card*.

remake.verb type: action — dynamic: making a new version of a film or song, rebuilding something from scratch (*remake the kitchen*), or transforming a person or institution (*remake the party*).
remake.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory — ✗ *Studios remake constantly* needs an object. The reflexive is normal in the transforming sense: *he remade himself after the divorce*.
remake.passive: **yes** — *that thriller has been remade twice already*; *the whole intersection has been remade since June*; *the party was remade from the ground up*.

repay.verb type: action — dynamic: returning money (*repay the loan*), returning a kindness (*repay your generosity*), requiting with harm (*repay their trust with a lawsuit*), and — with a thing as subject — being worth the effort (*the book repays careful reading*).
repay.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory — the object may be the person (*I'll repay you*), the debt (*repay the loan*), or the kindness. Marginally ditransitive (*repay him the money*); the usual frames are *repay X for Y* and *repay X with Y*.
repay.passive: **yes** in the money and favor senses — *the loan was repaid in eighteen months*; *every favor the family had done them had been repaid*. **Restricted** in the 'be worth the effort' sense: ? *Careful reading is repaid by the book* is awkward.

say.verb type: action — dynamic, the basic verb of speech (*say something*), extended to what a text or instrument indicates (*the sign says the pool closes at nine*), to reported common belief (*they say the pass is closed*), and to what something conveys (*her silence said more than an argument*).
say.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is normally a clause (*she said she would call back*) or a noun (*say nothing*, *say grace*). Never ditransitive: the addressee takes *to* — *say something to someone*, ✗ *He said me the news* (that frame belongs to *tell*).
say.passive: **yes** — *nothing was said about a deadline*; and the impersonal raising passive is standard journalism: *he is said to have turned down the job twice*. The addressee can never be the passive subject: ✗ *I was said the news.*

ski.verb type: action — dynamic: traveling over snow on skis, both as the sport and as a means of getting somewhere.
ski.transitivity: **both** — normally intransitive with no object at all (*we ski every weekend*, *my father still skis at seventy-two*), transitive with a run or a mountain as object (*they skied the back bowls*, *ski a black diamond*).
ski.passive: **restricted** — no passive of the intransitive *we ski every weekend*. The transitive passive is possible but confined to skiers' talk: *that face had never been skied before that winter*.

underlay.verb type: action — dynamic: putting a layer of something underneath for support or cushioning (*underlay the carpet with padding*), including the technical printing and music uses.
underlay.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory, in the frame *underlay A with B*. Careful: *the assumptions that underlay the plan* is the past of a different verb, *underlie*.
underlay.passive: **yes** — *the carpet was underlaid with thick padding*; *the tile had been underlaid with the wrong material entirely*; *the whole second floor has been underlaid with cork*.

underpay.verb type: action — dynamic: paying a worker less than the work is worth (*underpay the kitchen staff*), or paying less than the amount actually due (*underpay your estimated taxes*).
underpay.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the worker or the amount as object (*the company underpaid her for three years*), intransitive when the object is understood (*if you underpay, you owe a penalty*).
underpay.passive: **yes**, and it is the commoner form — *substitute teachers have been underpaid for a decade*; *dozens of workers had been underpaid*. The participle is the standard adjective in *overworked and underpaid*.

unmake.verb type: action — dynamic, but formal and largely literary: undoing what was made (*time has unmade the treaty*) or destroying a person's standing (*a scandal can unmake a career*).
unmake.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory, and typically set against *make*: *what the legislature makes, the legislature unmakes*.
unmake.passive: **yes**, though context has to carry it — *the treaty was unmade piece by piece*; *he was unmade by the same voters who made him*. Beware the ordinary adjective: *the bed was unmade* means it was never made, not that someone un-made it.

unsay.verb type: action — dynamic, a speech act, but almost frozen in the recognition that it cannot be performed: *you cannot unsay a thing like that*.
unsay.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory — *unsay a word*, *unsay every claim in his statement*.
unsay.passive: **yes**, and the passive is where the verb actually lives — *what's said cannot be unsaid*; *once a rumor is out, it is never unsaid*. Note that the bare adjective *unsaid* means 'never spoken at all' — *some things are better left unsaid* — nearly the opposite.

waylay.verb type: action — dynamic: intercepting someone on their way, today usually just to corner them in conversation (*waylay the senator outside the chamber*), historically to ambush and rob them.
waylay.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory and almost always a person — ✗ *Reporters waylay every afternoon* is incomplete.
waylay.passive: **yes**, and the passive is at least as common as the active — *I was waylaid at the mailbox for twenty minutes*; *the supply column was waylaid at the pass*.
